nameStory: This goldenrod earned its "large-leaved" name from its impressively oversized leaves, which can stretch up to 6 inches long — much bigger than most of its golden cousins. While many goldenrods have narrow, skinny leaves, this northern beauty stands out with foliage that's bold and broad. The scientific name "macrophylla" literally means "big leaf" in Latin, so botanists were thinking the same thing!
description: Large-leaved goldenrod is a sturdy perennial wildflower that can grow up to 3.5 feet tall, making it a medium-sized member of the goldenrod family. What makes it special are those notably large, broad leaves that give it its name, paired with clusters of bright yellow flower heads in late summer. Unlike the massive plume-like flower displays of some goldenrods, this species produces its 100+ tiny yellow blooms mostly along shorter side branches. It's a hardy northern plant that thrives in cooler climates, even growing north of the Arctic Circle in some places.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The star feature — leaves are remarkably large for a goldenrod, up to 6 inches long and notably broad with a smooth, soft texture when you run your fingers along them. They're arranged alternately up the stem and have a fresh, green smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright yellow flower heads cluster along short side branches rather than forming one big showy plume. Each tiny flower head contains multiple even tinier flowers, and one plant can produce over 100 of these golden clusters.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a sturdy, upright perennial reaching up to 42 inches tall with a thick, woody underground stem (rhizome) that feels solid and substantial if you dig around the base.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: The stem is typically green to reddish-brown and feels firm and somewhat ridged to the touch, much sturdier than many other wildflowers.

habitat: Look for large-leaved goldenrod in cooler, northern areas of New England, especially in moist woodlands, forest edges, and mountain slopes. It prefers partially shaded spots with rich, moist soil and is more common at higher elevations. You'll often find it growing alongside other northern forest plants like wild ginger and trilliums.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge with those distinctive large leaves beginning to unfurl, making identification possible even without flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time in late summer when clusters of bright yellow flowers appear along the side branches, buzzing with bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into fluffy, white seed heads that catch the wind, while leaves may turn golden-yellow before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, but the woody rhizome remains alive underground, ready to send up new shoots in spring.

funFact: Some populations of large-leaved goldenrod grow north of the Arctic Circle in Quebec and Labrador — making it one of the few goldenrods tough enough to bloom under the midnight sun!
confusionNotes: The large leaves make this goldenrod pretty distinctive, but it could be confused with broad-leaved goldenrod. Remember: large-leaved has flowers on short side branches, while broad-leaved has flowers in a more open, branched cluster. Think "large leaves, little branches" for this species!
contextualKnowledge: Despite having "goldenrod" in the name, this plant doesn't cause hay fever — that's actually ragweed blooming at the same time! Goldenrods have heavy pollen that doesn't blow around much, while ragweed produces the lightweight pollen that makes people sneeze.
compareHints: Among New England goldenrods, large-leaved stands out immediately for its broad foliage — most others like Canada goldenrod and field goldenrod have much narrower, more lance-shaped leaves. The flower arrangement is also different, with blooms on short side branches rather than the big, showy plumes of tall goldenrod or the flat-topped clusters of silverrod.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's goldenrods, wrinkle-leaved goldenrod stands out for its distinctly rough, sandpapery leaves - most others like Canada goldenrod or giant goldenrod have smooth foliage.
Among New England's 25+ goldenrod species, seaside goldenrod stands out with its thick, fleshy leaves and coastal habitat - most other goldenrods have thin, papery leaves and prefer inland locations.
Among its 25+ goldenrod cousins in New England, silverrod is unmistakable due to its white flowers.
Among the 26 goldenrod species in New England, bluestem is unique for its blue-purple stem and woodland habitat preference.
Among the 25+ goldenrod species in New England, broad-leaved goldenrod is unique in its woodland habitat and zigzag stem.
Among New England's many goldenrods, early goldenrod stands out for its July bloom time and graceful, arching flower plumes.
Among New England's many goldenrods, Canada goldenrod is distinguished by its gracefully arching, plume-like flower clusters and smooth stems.
Among New England's many goldenrods, field goldenrod stands out for being one of the shortest and grayest.
Among New England's many goldenrods, giant goldenrod stands out for its impressive height — it's typically the tallest species you'll encounter.
Among New England's many goldenrods, downy goldenrod is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture on both stems and leaves.
Cutler's goldenrod is much shorter and more compact than common lowland species like Canada goldenrod or tall goldenrod, which can reach 6 feet or more.
Among New England's goldenrods, tall goldenrod stands out for its impressive height and pyramid-shaped flower clusters.
Among New England's many goldenrods, sweet goldenrod is the only one with that distinctive anise fragrance - this makes it the easiest goldenrod to identify with certainty.
Among New England's many goldenrods, bog goldenrod stands out for its wetland habitat requirement and impressive height.
Among New England's many goldenrods, squarrose goldenrod stands out for its exceptionally narrow, elongated flower cluster that stays tightly upright rather than spreading outward.
Among New England's 26 goldenrod species, swamp goldenrod is unique for its wetland habitat - no other goldenrod in our region specifically seeks out waterlogged soils.

Among New England's many goldenrods, cut-leaf goldenrod stands out for its preference for woodland settings rather than open fields, and its more delicate, open flower arrangement compared to the dense, plume-like clusters of field-loving species like Canada goldenrod.
Among New England's goldenrods, Elliott's stands out for its exceptional height and strict coastal marsh habitat - most other goldenrods prefer drier upland sites.
Among New England's many goldenrods, showy goldenrod stands out for its impressive height and dense, pyramid-shaped flower clusters.

Among New England's many goldenrods, hairy goldenrod stands out for its distinctly rough, bristly texture - much more pronounced than the slight fuzziness of Canada goldenrod or the smooth stems of giant goldenrod.

Among New England's many goldenrods, stiff-leaved goldenrod stands out for its flat-topped flower clusters (versus the branching plumes of Canada goldenrod or tall goldenrod) and especially its thick, rigid leaves that feel completely different from the soft, flexible foliage of common species.
Unlike its yellow-flowered goldenrod cousins that typically have branching, plume-like flower clusters, white flat-topped goldenrod has distinctively flat, white flower heads.
Unlike the abundant Canada Goldenrod or Giant Goldenrod with their large, spreading flower clusters, Sticky Goldenrod has more compact, narrow flower heads.
Among New England goldenrods, elm-leaved goldenrod is unique for its broad, elm-like leaves - most others like Canada goldenrod and tall goldenrod have narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's many goldenrods, racemose goldenrod is unique for its simple, unbranched flower spike - all other regional goldenrods have branching flower clusters.
Rand's goldenrod differs from common goldenrods by its specialized rocky mountain habitat and extreme rarity.
